content.thinking:
I need to plan the whole module carefully before writing, drawing on the builder API, paints, SVG texture, and glow kit I've reviewed. I'm sketching gnome proportions: roughly 0.85 m body with a pointy hat bringing total height to about 1.2 m.

I'm envisioning a whimsical, faceted low-poly style with flat colors and cheerful tones, using low segment counts and disabled smoothing on sweeps for that chunky faceted look. For the skeleton I'm planning a hip root with spine, neck, head, and jaw joints, arms with shoulder-elbow-wrist chains plus simplified finger/thumb digits, legs with hip-knee-ankle-toe chains, and I'm still figuring out how to structure the beard joints since the available roles don't map cleanly onto a beard chain.

Now I'm sketching out additional joints: a floppy hat tip chain, a backpack attached to the spine with a hinged lid, plus small details like an antenna, crank, and gear, all using hinge roles. I'm being careful with the TypeScript since I can't typecheck as I go, so I'm planning to use explicit absolute coordinates and bone references for simplicity rather than relying on local joint space, and I'm working out the vertical layout in meters—placing the feet at floor level, ankles, knees, and hips at specific heights to keep the gnome's proportions short-legged and chunky, aiming for a total height around 1.15 meters with the hat.

I'm refining the full vertical layout—feet, knees, hips, round belly, shoulders, neck, and a large head—then adding a conical hat that droops backward, adjusting heights downward slightly so the total figure lands closer to 1.25 meters instead of ballooning past 1.4.

Now I'm settling on a cheerful color palette under 64 colors, defining rosy skin tones, a nose and cheek blush, and red hat shades with highlight and shadow variants.

For the clothing I'm picking a beige beard tone, a teal tunic, brown leather apron, mustard trousers, and brown boots to give the gnome a warm, cheerful look.

Still finalizing color palette...

I'm thinking through how to render surface details like tunic stripes, hat textures, and simple low-poly eyes using basic sphere and highlight shapes.

Adding brass goggles with glowing teal lenses, then planning a loaded backpack frame packed with bellows, gears, a spyglass, lantern, springs, tools, a propeller, antenna, gauge, and other tinkerer gear, aiming for roughly 300-400 low-poly parts total while staying under 1000. Now I'm setting up the builder function with flat geometry enabled.

Writing geometry helpers...

Still writing gear geometry...

Now building the skeleton joints and chains—starting with a hips root joint and working out a spine chain with intermediate points, making sure the chain's starting position lines up sensibly with the hips joint rather than overlapping awkwardly.

For the spine tip's parent, I should reference the last joint explicitly since chain parenting defaults might not resolve correctly. Then for the neck and head, I'm considering simplifying by defining joints directly instead of using chains, setting the head joint's parent and aim based on the neck's endpoint.

Now I'm working out the jaw joint, positioning it under the head with its own aim direction, and thinking through how the beard and mustache should attach -- the mustache covering most of the mouth while the beard flows down from the jaw or head, with a small movable chin piece for an open mouth effect.

I'm sketching head proportions: a flattened sphere for the skull, a rosy nose protruding forward, small eyes, bushy brows, pointed ears jutting out, and a hat resting on top -- all placed with specific coordinates and sizes to get the gnome's face right.

Now I'm placing the jaw and lower face: a hinge point under the head leading to the chin, with a small jaw mass mostly hidden by the beard, and a tiny dark mouth shape positioned just beneath where the mustache will sit.

For the arms, I'm setting shoulder joints slightly out from the torso in a relaxed A-pose, then computing elbow and wrist positions by extending outward and downward with consistent segment lengths for the upper arm and forearm.

I want the arm chain to include a hand tip joint at the end, so I'm using four names (shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand) against a three-point path, letting the extra name create a terminal tip joint for the hand.

I'll follow the usual hip/knee/ankle pattern for the arm: names ["shoulderL","elbowL","handL"] along path S,E,W, with the hand joint sitting at the wrist. For the tube sweep I'll taper the arm radius from 0.045 to 0.04, give the sleeve a teal tube with a cuff ring at the wrist, and add tan mitten-shaped hands with separate thumb and finger digit chains.

For hands I'll keep it simple: a fingers chain with 3 points (f1,f2,f3 tip) and a thumb chain with 2 points (t1,t2), plus a palm ball offset slightly from the wrist to anchor both sweeps, all in tan to match the glove mitts.

I'll give the mitten a wide ellipse shape with a few knuckle bumps for whimsical, oversized hands. Rather than having the gnome grip anything, I'll keep the arms neutral and skip hand-held items, maybe putting a wrench on the belt instead. Now moving to legs, I'm placing the hip, knee, and ankle joints along the chain.

Adding toe and boot joints...

I'll add a dark sole slab beneath the foot sphere so the lowest contact point sits right at y=0, keeping the boot geometry properly grounded on the floor.

For the torso, I'm planning a loft from hips to chest using faceted stations bound to the spine chain, with the hips joint anchoring the base position.

I'm now sketching the actual station widths and depths going up the torso — narrow at the waist, flaring out for the belly, then narrowing again toward the chest, since the depth axis runs front-to-back along the frame normal.

For the shoulders and neck I'm keeping the top stations tighter and noting the loft needs to extend slightly past where the spine bone chain ends. For the tunic coloring, I'm setting up a paint function that blends a darker and lighter teal based on vertical position to create a subtle gradient effect on the garment.

I'll apply the paint gradients to the larger surfaces like the tunic, trousers, hat, and backpack, keeping smaller details as flat colors to balance texel density, staying true to a hand-painted low-poly look with flat-shaded facets plus smooth gradients. Now I'm sketching the hat as a swept cone shape along a curved path, bending the pointy tip backward for that droopy wizard-hat silhouette.

Working out the hat's joint chain, radius falloff, and faceted cone geometry, I'm also adding a small folded brim band near the hat's base to account for where it sits on the head, checking the head's top height to make sure the hat aligns correctly.

Checking the hat radius against the head radius at each height confirms good coverage, so I'll tilt the hat slightly back for a jaunty rakish angle.

Adjusting hat position and angle...

I'm reconsidering the brim size since a wide disc would overshadow the eyebrows and eyes awkwardly — I should keep the brim narrower so it sits above the face without hiding key features.

Now I'm sketching the pointy elf-gnome ears as a separate outline shape positioned outward from the head, extruded along the x-axis so they jut out and curve slightly upward and back below the hat.

I'm working out the cone's local axis orientation and using an `up` hint so its flattened dimension aligns with the front-back direction, scaling local z by about 0.35 to make it a thin ear-like plate.

Now I'm adding the inner pink ear detail as a smaller, slightly offset version, then moving on to the nose as a rosy flattened sphere with a small highlight, and placing blush discs on the cheeks while checking their positioning against the head ellipsoid's surface so they sit flush rather than floating or clipping.

Working out eye placement: center around z .165-.185, with a dark glossy sphere plus small white highlight for a whimsical cartoon look, or alternatively sclera plus pupil sized for a big-eyed effect. I'll go with layered whites, pupils, and highlights facing forward, then move on to designing bushy brow sweeps.

Now I'm positioning the brow rods tapering along the forehead curve, calculating surface z-depth so they sit naturally under the brim without clipping, using tapered radius and rounded caps for a soft look.

For the mustache I'm sweeping a handlebar curve under the nose using a Catmull path from left curl tip through center to right tip, nudging it lower and thicker so it bulges out and tucks under the nose's overlap without poking through the head surface.

For the beard, I'm planning a chain of segments hanging from the jaw down the chest, defining a center-line path from jaw to belly and then lofting a pointed V-shape with the width tapering along stations down its length.

I'm checking the beard path clears the torso and belly at each height, verifying it hangs slightly in front of the belly without clipping. Working out the actual coordinate points for the beard curve from top to tip.

I should shorten the beard so it ends around y=0.50 rather than reaching the belt, picking five waypoints with decreasing station widths toward the tip, and I'm considering adding small cheek tufts near the ears plus a couple of overlapping shorter beard layers for texture.

For beard texture, I'll apply grained hair-streak coloring along the y-axis instead of flat leaf shapes, and I'm thinking about adding brass beads or a ring at the beard's end, plus a dark grease smudge decal on the cheek for a tinkerer vibe. I'll also place brass goggles on the hat's front above the brim, with two lenses positioned near y=1.03.

Working out the hat's cone geometry to position the goggles correctly...

Now I'm placing goggles on the hat front near y≈1.04-1.045, figuring the hat surface radius there and positioning lens cylinders along a slightly backward-tilted axis with a brass tube and inset lens disc for each eye.

For the goggle strap band wrapping around the hat, I'm computing the right radius for a lathe-generated ring near y=1.0, accounting for the hat's slight tilt so the band clears the cone surface at the back rather than intersecting it.

I'm also thinking through extra hat details—maybe a small stitched patch decal, a tiny brass bell at the tip, or a feather for a tinkerer vibe.

Adding a little gear pinned to the hat's side and a pencil behind the ear for a cute, whimsical touch. For the hat's coloring, I'm considering layered stripe paints in varying reds with some wobble and shading to give it a knit, textured look despite the drooping tip.

Now moving to the body: a teal tunic over mustard trousers with a brown apron, keeping the palette cheerful and varied. For the tunic hem, I'm flaring it out over the hips with a lofted bottom, possibly adding a scalloped or dagged skirt edge using a lathe profile for extra visual interest.

Checking proportions so the skirt radius covers the thighs without hiding too much of the trousers, with the hem ending around the knee area before the boot cuffs begin.

I'll skip scalloped dags and keep it simple with 8-segment low-poly geometry, adding a cream trim band at the hem with painted stripe detail. For the belt, I'm thinking through how to generate a loop around the torso at the hip level, using a surface loft with a slight lift so it sits naturally over the torso mesh.

For the buckle, I need to raycast from the belt line to find the front surface point, then stick a brass box there, handling the null case safely. But I realize the beard tip hangs down to around that same height and would hide the buckle, so I should shift the belt slightly lower to keep it visible.

Now I'm thinking through the tool belt accessories—pouches, a wrench, hammer, screwdriver loops, tape measure—positioning them around the belt ring using polar coordinates based on the torso's elliptical cross-section at that height.

For the apron, I'm considering how to drape a brown leather bib against the curved torso, deciding between a loft or sweep approach to get the panel to hug the body naturally.

I'm checking whether a flat apron plate would float off the belly's lateral curve, and figuring the gap is small enough to hide by narrowing the plate and thickening it slightly, or alternatively draping a membrane between the two edges for a better fit.

I should use more sample points along each edge path, maybe six per side, so draping catches the curve properly, with points placed slightly outside the surface so each one snaps inward to the nearest front point. I need to check the apron's bib and hem placement relative to the beard overlay and belt, since draping should only apply to the torso loft itself.

Then I realize the skirt is a separate mesh, so the surface target needs to include both torso and skirt parts for accurate draping of the lower apron hem. Given the complexity, I decide it's too risky to fully verify bone weighting and drape behavior for such a large module without testing, so I'll keep the fallback approach minimal and move forward cautiously.

Weighing the risk of exotic APIs against reliability, I settle on using the more battle-tested primitives — part, sweep, loft, lathe, extrude, rod — rather than attempting a membrane-based apron. Instead I'll model the apron as a simple extruded flat plate with curvature approximated through placement and thickness, checking that the gap between the plate edges and the belly surface stays small enough to be visually acceptable.

Since the belly contour isn't actually planar (narrower and flatter higher up, bulging lower), I think the safest approach is sweeping a box-sectioned path along a catmull curve that follows the belly's front profile, offsetting slightly outward so the plate hugs the surface with minimal gap at the edges.

Now I'm working out the front-face stations along the apron path: for each y position I'm tracking z, width, and height to derive the front offset (center z plus half-height) at that station.

Continuing stations, I'm also noting the shoulder joints extend outside the torso width at that height, so I'll add puffy sleeve-cap spheres bridging torso to arms for the tunic look. Then I'm interpolating the apron plate's front-z path between stations using simple linear blending at intermediate y values.

The apron needs to rest on top of the skirt rather than float, so below the belt I'm shrinking the apron's extent and letting the skirt's own flare (growing to about .2 radius at the hem) take over the silhouette, keeping the apron bottom around y .40 where the skirt is just starting to widen.

Actually, simpler to drop the lathed skirt flare entirely and just let the tunic hem end near y .40 as the torso loft's bottom edge, flaring the lower torso station wider, then transitioning into mustard trousers below with a hem band loop for the tunic edge rather than relathing.

Defining apron stations...

I'll bind a torso bone list combining hips and spine for shared torso items, confirming the bone type accepts a joint, chain, or array of either. Then I'm adding an apron pocket patch near the plate front, giving the apron a mottled leather stain texture, and starting shoulder strap sweeps running from the top corners.

Working out strap curve points...

Now I'm sizing the backpack placement behind the torso, positioning it large and centered on the gnome's back since the whimsical style calls for an oversized pack, while figuring out its width, height, and depth to span correctly without clipping through the body.

Building the pack as a tapered box shape...

For texture I'll use mottling and stripes to suggest painted canvas. I'll rig the pack to a joint on spine2, with a separate hinged lid joint at the back-top edge so the flap can open upward.

Still positioning pack parts...

For gadgets attached to the pack, I'm adding a lashed telescoping spyglass on the left side, a copper kettle hanging on the right, a pair of meshing gear cogs mounted on the back as an animated hinge joint, and a telescopic antenna rod with a glowing bulb rising above the pack.

On top I'm adding a small spinning propeller mast as a hinge joint, plus a pressure gauge dial on the back rendered as a textured plane, and an accordion-style bellows on the right made from alternating wood-toned cylinder segments with end plates and a nozzle.

Then I'm layering in more charm: spiral coil springs on the lower back, a swinging lantern joint on the left with a glass glow cage and brass hardware, a copper pipe sweep with elbow joints and a little puff of steam spheres for storytelling, plus strapped tools like wrenches, a hammer, a funnel, a hanging key tag, a crank handle hinge, and small cog trinkets.

I'm also adding glowing liquid vials in side pockets, a rolled blueprint scroll tube with a red ribbon, and deciding to skip extra critters like a clockwork bird or spider to keep scope manageable. Given the growing complexity, I want to build helper functions to avoid geometry mistakes, and I'm mapping out the full joint hierarchy for the pack and rig -- pack lid hinge, gear hinges, prop and crank hinges, lantern hinge -- alongside the core skeleton of hips, spine segments, neck, head, jaw, and arms.

I'm tallying total joint count across fingers, thumbs, legs, toes, beard, hat chain, and pack, landing around 55, and setting up a mirror helper to generate left/right side names symmetrically. I also need to keep the flat color palette under 64 and plan small decorative SVG textures -- a gauge dial, a stitched patch, maybe a blueprint label or crate sticker -- all with transparent backgrounds.

Writing SVG code...

I'll skip svg eye decals and go with 3D eyes instead, giving gloves a tan color and teal sleeves with cream cuffs. Now I'm checking the part function's signature to make sure colors and options are typed correctly before writing more section code.

I'm settling on always passing options objects with color and radius for sweep calls, and confirming the returned Sweep type exposes meshes so glow effects work. For lathe parts I'm defining a helper that takes an outline array of points plus placement, bone, color, and segment count to generate rotational shapes.

Now I'm working out extrude's options shape with thickness and bevel, and checking how rod sweeps use sides/smooth flags to control faceting versus smoothness for low-poly tube geometry. I'm also noting how textures get loaded via the svg helper and how flat planes get placed with position, direction, and axis options, plus using flat:true on parts to keep surfaces faceted rather than smoothed.

Writing small vector utility functions...

I should also confirm Fill assignability covers string|Paint fine, and that bone parameters should be typed as Joint, importing that type from the skeleton module so chain joints like spine.joints[i] type-check correctly. Now I want to work through each part with actual coordinates, writing compactly but with enough detail.

I need to stay disciplined about unused imports since those cause errors—every import I bring in needs to actually get used. For gear geometry I'll rely on ExtrudeGeometry with teeth already built into the shape, skipping any geometry merging utilities since they're unnecessary here. I'm sketching out the paint types I'll need: gradient, grain, mottle, patches, stripes, countershade, mix, and noise/smoothstep helpers.

Writing SVG markup...

I'm working out the trigonometry for a gauge SVG—computing arc endpoints at specific angles (210°, 130°, 50°, -30°) around a center point with radius 22, converting between math-angle convention and SVG's y-down coordinate system to place the green, yellow, and red zone arcs correctly along the gauge's sweep.

Now I'm defining the needle direction with its tip computed from an angle and a hub circle, adding tick marks, and planning a separate hat/patch icon using a rounded rectangle and gear shape.

Now sketching a blueprint-style icon instead: a blue background with faint grid lines and schematic circles representing a gear and wing outline, adjusting stroke widths for a clean technical-drawing look at the new canvas size.

I'm reconsidering the small details—folded corners, hanging tags, and jar labels—weighing whether to add text like "No.7" versus keeping it purely graphical to avoid font rendering issues, and thinking through how a label texture would wrap around a cylinder's UV coordinates.

I'm settling on a cream label texture with scribbled lines and a red dot for the jars, plus striped paint along the bedroll's axis and cream discs for its spiral ends. Now I'm starting the actual builder code, defining joints like the hips as the spine root for the gnome tinkerer figure.

Building spine chain and head joints...

Checking segment lengths from shoulder to elbow to wrist, tapering arm radii, and placing the mitten hand near the wrist with the arms hanging outward at roughly 35 degrees.

I'm setting up the arm chains as joint hierarchies parented to the spine, figuring out which spine joint sits closest to the shoulder height so the arms attach naturally near the top of the torso.

I'm defining the three-point polyline for shoulder-elbow-hand, choosing a hard-cornered polyline over a smooth catmull curve, then sweeping a tapered six-sided tube along it to form the sleeve geometry.

Now I'm working out finger and thumb joints off the wrist tip—placing knuckle points that curl slightly forward for the fingers, and positioning the thumb so it faces inward/forward matching a natural hanging-hand pose.

For the finger chain I'm defining a mitten-style sweep that tapers the tube width while flattening it front-to-back, keeping fingers wide in x but thin in z so they read as a mitten rather than individual digits, then adding a palm sphere to blend everything at the wrist.

Now I'm reconsidering whether to separate the hand into 3 distinct fingers plus a thumb for better rigging clarity, which means setting up 3 two-joint chains (index, middle, ring) spread across x at the knuckle row, alongside the existing thumb chain.

Working out the finger geometry...

Adjusting the cuff position slightly up along the arm axis so it sits right at the sleeve edge, then adding a shoulder pad sphere sunk into the torso at the shoulder joint. Now I'm working out the leg joint positions, placing hip, knee, and ankle points down the leg path.

Setting up the trouser taper radii and sides, defining the ankle and toe joints with aim targets for the foot direction, and sketching the boot shaft and front cylinder dimensions along the lower leg.

Still placing boot geometry...

I'm skipping laces and adding a darker strap band with a brass buckle near the ankle, then verifying floor contact so the sole and sphere components sit flush at y=0 without clipping. I'm also checking that the trouser hem tucks cleanly inside the boot shaft opening before moving on to the torso loft and tunic details like hem trim and front buttons.

I'm adding small tan elbow patches, giving the tunic subtle horizontal knit stripes with countershading so the back reads lighter than the belly, then sweeping a short neck segment to connect head and torso, mostly hidden by the beard.

Now I'm building the head: a scaled sphere for the skull shape, painted with a countershaded skin tone so the face reads warmer and ruddier toward the lower jaw, followed by a small scaled sphere for the nose.

I'm positioning the nose so it protrudes whimsically beyond the face, giving it a rosy flat color plus a tiny pale highlight sphere for shine. Then I'm placing the mustache just under the nose, overlapping slightly, and tucking the mouth as a tiny hidden dark shape beneath it near where the beard begins.

Now I'm building out the jaw and chin — a lower lip sphere, a skin-colored chin ball, and beard sideburn tufts attached to the sides of the head to frame the face.

Now I'm shaping the ears as flattened cones angled outward and upward from the head, working out the orientation so the cone's thickness axis aligns properly with the skull's surface normal.

I consider adding a smaller pinkish inner-ear cone offset slightly forward for depth. I also think about tucking a pencil behind the right ear, but the hat brim collides with that placement at that height, so I decide to skip it and move the pencil to the belt instead.

I'm angling the pencil so it pokes through the hat at a slant, running from inside the surface out toward the front-up direction. Then I'm positioning goggles on the hat's front, calculating the lens centers against the cone surface and figuring out the normal direction so they sit flush against the tilted hat.

Still placing goggle components...

Still computing patch placement...

Now I'm setting up the hat's bone chain with joints from the head through several hat segments, defining parent-child relationships for the sweep spans.

I'm sweeping the chain into a smooth bending cone mesh with flat and pointed caps, then defining the hat's paint pattern with stripes, countershading, and a gradient toward the tip.

A small brass bell sphere sits at the hat's tip, attached to the last joint, while a lathed brim ring with an outlined profile adds the red-dark flat-colored brim at the base of the head bone, positioned with a slight forward z offset.

I'm skipping extra hair tufts since the brim covers them, focusing instead on eye geometry: scaled white spheres positioned at the head surface, pupils as smaller spheres offset forward with reduced z-scale, and tiny highlight spheres layered on top for shine.

Now I'm placing rosy cheek blush discs tangent to the facial curve with a coral tint, calculating normals and positions along the skull's surface, and considering whether to add a small soot smudge to one cheek for character.

I decide to skip the smudge detail and rely on apron stains for grime instead. Now I'm moving on to the backpack, defining its joint position in model coordinates attached to the spine's second joint.

Working out backpack frustum dimensions...

I want to soften the blocky shape with rounded edges, maybe adding thin cylindrical trim rods along the vertical edges and top/bottom rims for a leather-piping look. Now I'm considering which faces need detail (back, sides, lid) and picking a color—leaning toward an olive-green tone around "#8a9a4b" for the canvas.

I'm thinking of giving the pack a quilted patchwork treatment instead of a plain canvas texture, using a brown stitch-line base with varied patch colors like olive, sand, mustard, and rust to create a whimsical patterned pack rather than something too uniform or garish.

Now I'm working out the lid geometry — positioning and hinging it to the pack body, then adding thin brass buckle straps that wrap over the lid front down to the sides for a functional closure detail.

Lid hinges at z -.385. I'm defining a back-surface offset for mounting attachments, then placing two meshing gears on the pack back—a bigger copper one and a smaller one—working out the center-to-center distance needed so their teeth overlap correctly based on their radii.

Still placing attachments...

I'm adding a vent tube with small white puff spheres and translucent steam clouds at the pipe's end, then reworking the back-face layout to avoid overlap, positioning the big gear and spring components across the x/y grid.

Still checking gear-to-gauge spacing and pipe routing...

Adding a vertical spring coil near the bottom right, around x .12, with four turns and a small pitch to keep its height compact so it fits alongside the pipe path.

Now I'm working out the side placements: crank on the left side, bellows on the right with its axis along z, wooden end discs, leather accordion ribs via a zigzag lathe, and a brass nozzle pointing backward, roughly centered around (.225, .63, -.26) with about .22 length.

I'm adding small strap boxes connecting the pack to the bellows, then positioning the lantern hanging below on the left side via a hook and chain joint, with the cage body sitting around (.215, .40, -.30) — checking it clears the bellows bottom, the thigh, and the hand position without overlap.

Now I'm working on the right side: placing a copper kettle hanging from pack straps near (-.225, .50, -.27), and adding a crank mechanism with a hinge joint, hub, arm, and handle around (-.18, .72, -.30) with its axis along -x. I'm also sketching a bedroll positioned horizontally across the top of the pack around y .90.

I'm adding leather straps (thin rings) securing the bedroll, then placing an antenna mast at the back-left top, running from base (.11,.85,-.34) upward, checking it clears the bedroll's footprint. I'm debating whether the mast should be parented to the pack lid or mounted separately on a base plate so it doesn't swing awkwardly when the lid opens.

Simplifying by mounting the bedroll, antenna, and propeller all to the packLid joint so they ride naturally with the lid during its hinge animation. For the propeller, I'm setting a mast with a hub and two blades lying in the xz-plane, extruded with thickness oriented along the right axes so the blade shape stays elongated properly.

I'm redesigning this as three symmetric blades at rotated angles, verifying the perpendicular axis math so each blade's thickness still points vertically, and planning alternating cream and red coloring for a whimsical look.

I'm now positioning the prop's mounting point and the antenna's glowing bulb tip, then working through where to strap the spyglass on the pack without overlapping the pipe or gauge, settling on running it vertically along the pack's left edge instead.

Good, no overlap there. Now I'm placing the spyglass tube as three telescoping cylinder segments with decreasing radii, stacked vertically near x .135, keeping it straight rather than tilted.

I'm adding leather straps and brass rings around the spyglass, plus a glowing teal lens disc at the top eyepiece. Then shifting to a pipe at x -.16 and considering adding a wrench, hammer, and crates near the pack's lower belt area, along with front shoulder straps running from the pack top down to the chest.

Working out backpack strap geometry...

Mapping out the strap geometry, I decide to simplify to just an over-shoulder path down to a front buckle near the belt rather than a full complex loop under the arm, plotting rough coordinates for the shoulder-to-chest curve.

I reconsider the apron straps entirely—since the beard covers the neck area, I drop them and let the backpack straps carry the visual weight instead, with the bib simply hanging from a neck ring. Now I'm working out the strap tube's cross-section and orientation so it flattens naturally against the body surface.

Now adding torso details: a collar under the beard, brass buttons on the bib, and a bib pocket with tools poking out—screwdriver, pencil, ruler, pliers. I'm sizing the pocket box and positioning the tools so their handles stick out above the pocket opening, rigging everything to the spine bone.

Next I'm working out the tool belt: pouches placed at angles around the hips, with a hammer hanging from a loop at the right hip, its steel head near the belt and wooden handle dangling down the thigh.

Now I'm shaping a wrench to hang from the left hip, defining its outline as a polygon with a notched open-end jaw at the head and a straight handle shaft.

Confirming the outline runs counter-clockwise, then I'm working out the extrusion orientation so the wrench hangs head-down from the hip with its flat face normal pointing outward, placing it at that belt position.

For the hammer on the opposite hip, I'm positioning the handle rod and a boxy steel head oriented horizontally at the top, planning to add a small claw detail. Then I'm figuring out symmetric placement for pouches at roughly ±50 degrees around the belt.

Still working through belt accessories... I'm also planning a belt loop by cutting a small ring around the torso loft at the belt line, then sweeping a thin hexagonal profile along it for the actual belt strap, plus raycasting to place a buckle on the front.

Using the moved frame offset so the second stick sits raised along the normal for the buckle's inner plate. Then I'm adding a hem trim loop near the bottom with cream coloring, skipping collar details, and keeping skin flat-colored for the low-poly look. For the beard I'm using a loft bound to a bone chain parented to the jaw, with stations following the beard point array.

Still working out beard geometry...

Placing a grid of beard cones at the surface hits, skipping any missed rays. For the mustache I'm adding curled-up tips with a tapering radius array and faceted sides, positioning the path so it sits just below the nose without overlapping.

Eyes and eyelashes are settled; adding tan leather work gloves on the hands. For remaining details I'm planning the hat chain joints, skipping extra bangs under the brim, and adding small tool props like a wrench, screwdriver, and tape measure in the bib pocket — no ground plane needed since it's character-only. Now I'm writing the gear geometry helper function.

Building gear tooth points...

Extruding the shape with a hole, then checking that Three.js handles the hole winding order correctly during triangulation.

e part helper taking an outline, position, bone, and color for lathe-based geometry. I'm checking that glow effects work with flat colors but not painted materials, and settling on which imports I actually need—skipping rng since randomness isn't required here, just pulling in createBuilder and the OutlinePoint type.

Now I'm defining small vector math helpers for adding and normalizing points, plus geometry shortcuts for spheres, cylinders, and boxes to speed up part construction.

Building the builder function...

Confirming the rod signature accepts a radius as either a number or a tuple for tapering. Now I'm defining skin tone color constants for the palette.

Defining more color constants...

I'm setting up paint functions for skin, tunic, and trousers using countershading and striped patterns to add shading and texture variation.

Now defining paints for the pack (patchwork colors), apron (mottled leather), beard (grain texture), and bedroll (striped), reusing the tunic paint for sleeves.

I'm estimating painted texel density given total surface area to pick an appropriate resolution, then starting to code the torso's shape as a lofted mesh bound to the hips and spine bones.

Still writing torso loft code...

Adding belt loop and stud details...

Now I'm sketching the apron sweep path with its taper points, building out the shape coordinates.

Adding stitch detail along the bib edges...

Now I'm placing the apron pocket as a box positioned on the front face, with a darker flap, brass rivets, and tools like a screwdriver, pencil, and ruler sticking out of the top.

I also need a pencil and other small tools poking out nearby. But I realize the beard geometry would actually hide these pocket tools behind its width at that height, so I need to reposition the pocket and tools lower or to the sides where they'll stay visible.
